hints: Think about iodide as a reducing agent, not just concentrated sulfuric acid as an acid. How strong a reducer is $\text{I}^-$ compared to other halides?
Remember the first step makes $\text{HI}$, then $\text{HI}$ reduces sulfur from +6 in $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ down through $\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{S}$.
Ask yourself what is the final, most reduced sulfur product that only the very powerful reducer iodide can reach.
walkthrough:
**Start with the acid-base step**

Think of this gently in two parts. First, solid $\text{NaI}$ reacts as an acid-base reaction to make $\text{HI}$ gas.

$$\text{NaI} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{NaHSO}_4 + \text{HI}$$
In $\text{NaHSO}_4$ and $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, sulfur is still at +6, so no reduction yet.

**Spot the reducing power of iodide**

Now the key chemistry starts. $\text{I}^-$ from $\text{HI}$ is a very strong reducing agent, much stronger than $\text{Br}^-$ or $\text{Cl}^-$. It donates electrons to sulfur, so sulfur is reduced from +6 to lower oxidation numbers.

**List the sulfur reduction products**

With iodide, reduction goes all the way in stages. You get sulfur dioxide, then sulfur, then hydrogen sulfide.

$$\text{S (+6) in H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{SO}_2 \text{ (+4)} \rightarrow \text{S (0)} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{S (-2)}$$
The lowest value reached is -2 in $\text{H}_2\text{S}$, so that is the answer.

options.A: Correct and well spotted. Iodide is powerful enough to reduce concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ all the way to $\text{H}_2\text{S}$, where sulfur is $\text{S}^{2-}$ with oxidation number -2. This is lower than $\text{SO}_2$ (+4) and $\text{S}$ (0).
options.B: Not the lowest, this is a common stopping trap. Elemental sulfur, $\text{S}$ with oxidation number 0, is indeed formed, but iodide keeps reducing further to $\text{H}_2\text{S}$. Choosing 0 misses the final reduction step.
options.C: This is only the first reduction product. $\text{SO}_2$ with sulfur at +4 is formed by bromide and iodide, but iodide is stronger and goes further to $\text{S}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{S}$. This choice confuses the bromide reaction with the iodide reaction.
options.D: This ignores reduction completely. +6 is the oxidation number of sulfur in the starting $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ and in $\text{NaHSO}_4$ or $\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4$. The question asks for reduced sulfur-containing products like $\text{SO}_2$, $\text{S}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{S}$.
